questions.prompt: What is Google's native UI testing framework for Android apps?
questions.explanation: Espresso runs in the app's process for fast, synchronised Android UI tests. XCUITest is Apple's equivalent.

questions.prompt: The Android hardware or gesture Back action has no single universal equivalent on iOS, so navigation tests often differ between the platforms.
questions.explanation: iOS relies on in-app back buttons and edge-swipe gestures; Android has a system Back. Shared test cases need platform-specific steps here.

questions.prompt: Which tool installs an APK on a connected Android device from the command line?
questions.explanation: adb (Android Debug Bridge) installs and manages apps on devices and emulators. xcrun simctl manages iOS simulators.

questions.code: xcrun simctl privacy booted reset camera com.example.shop
options: Installs the app on the simulator
Revokes (resets) the camera permission for the app on the booted iOS simulator so the permission prompt appears again
questions.explanation: simctl privacy can grant, revoke or reset a privacy permission for an app on a simulator, which is useful to retest first-launch permission flows.

questions.prompt: A push notification test passes on the iOS Simulator but users on real iPhones never get notifications. What is a likely gap?
options: The simulator test injected a notification locally (e.g. simctl push), which bypasses APNs, real device tokens and certificates; test end-to-end on real devices with the APNs environment
Push does not work on iOS
questions.explanation: Simulated pushes verify the app's handling, not the delivery chain. Certificate, token or environment mismatches only show up with real devices and APNs.

questions.prompt: Which differences between Android and iOS commonly need separate test cases? Select all that apply.
options: Runtime permission dialogs and their wording/options
Background execution limits and app lifecycle behaviour
Store review and distribution (TestFlight vs Play testing tracks)
questions.explanation: Permissions, lifecycle and distribution differ by platform. Arithmetic in shared logic does not.

questions.prompt: Android 13 (API 33) introduced which permission that affects many apps' notification flows?
questions.explanation: From Android 13, apps must request POST_NOTIFICATIONS at runtime, so first-launch notification behaviour needs testing on 13+ and older versions.

questions.prompt: Your app uses one cross-platform codebase (e.g. React Native). Leadership wants to test only on Android to save time. What is your advice?
options: Shared code reduces but does not remove platform risk: native modules, permissions, rendering, keyboard and lifecycle differ, so keep a risk-based iOS set (critical journeys plus platform-specific features)
Test only in a desktop browser
questions.explanation: Cross-platform frameworks still render with native components and call platform APIs. A smaller but deliberate iOS suite covers the real platform risks.

questions.prompt: A crash happens only on some Android devices from one manufacturer when the app resumes from background. How do you investigate?
options: Ignore it; it is the manufacturer's fault

Reproduce on that device model/OS (real or device cloud), capture logcat around the resume, check vendor battery/background restrictions, and test with 'Don't keep activities' enabled to force process death
questions.explanation: OEM customisations often kill background processes aggressively. Logs plus forcing process death in developer options reproduce state-restoration bugs reliably.

coding.title: Platform-specific capabilities
coding.prompt:
Write `caps_for(platform, app_path, device_name, platform_version)` returning W3C Appium capabilities as a dict:

- Android: `platformName` `'Android'`, `appium:automationName` `'UiAutomator2'`
- iOS: `platformName` `'iOS'`, `appium:automationName` `'XCUITest'`
- Both: `appium:app`, `appium:deviceName`, `appium:platformVersion` from the arguments.

`platform` is case-insensitive (`'android'`, `'ios'`). Raise `ValueError` otherwise. Also raise `ValueError` if the app path does not end with `.apk`/`.aab` for Android or `.app`/`.ipa` for iOS.
coding.starter:
def caps_for(platform, app_path, device_name, platform_version):
    return {'platformName': platform}
coding.explanation: Each platform needs its own automation driver, and in Appium 2 non-standard capabilities must carry the appium: vendor prefix. Validating the file type catches a common mix-up (sending an .ipa to an Android session) before a slow session start fails with a vaguer error.
hints: Normalise the platform with lower() and pick name, driver and allowed extensions.
str.endswith accepts a tuple of suffixes.
Use the appium: prefix for every non-W3C capability.

tests.name: ios caps
tests.code:
c = caps_for('ios', 'Shop.app', 'iPhone 16', '18.2')
assert c['platformName'] == 'iOS' and c['appium:automationName'] == 'XCUITest', c
